item.title: Agent-based trading simulation using Google ADK and A2A protocol
item.description:
Agent-based trading simulation using Google ADK and A2A protocol

This project demonstrates an agent-based trading system simulation featuring distinct agents for trading logic and risk management, communicating via the Agent-to-Agent (A2A) protocol. It includes a web-based simulator UI to configure, run, and visualize trading strategy performance.

🔍 Overview

The system consists of three main services interacting via HTTP and the A2A protocol. It leverages the open A2A protocol for standardized, interoperable communication between the agents. This allows agents built with different frameworks to discover capabilities and interact securely. The entire system is built using the Google Agent Development Kit (ADK).

🧩 How it works

The workflow begins with the Simulator UI taking simulation parameters from the user. It then runs the market simulation loop. For each step, the Simulator calls the AlphaBot service via A2A tasks/send, providing current market data and portfolio state. AlphaBot analyzes the data to determine a potential trade signal. If a trade is proposed, AlphaBot calls the RiskGuard service with the trade proposal and portfolio state. RiskGuard evaluates the proposal against configured rules and returns an approval or rejection. The final trade decision is returned to the Simulator, which updates the portfolio state based on executed trades.

⚙️ Key details

  • AlphaBot: Implements a Simple Moving Average (SMA) crossover strategy to propose trades. It calculates SMAs to determine BUY or SELL signals and updates its internal state.
  • RiskGuard: Evaluates trade proposals against configurable risk rules, including max position size and max portfolio concentration.
  • Simulator UI: A FastAPI-based web application that allows users to configure parameters for market conditions (initial price, volatility, trend), trading strategy (SMA periods, trade quantity), and risk rules. It visualizes results using Plotly, displaying price action, SMA indicators, portfolio value, and trade execution markers on interactive charts.
  • Deployment: Includes scripts for easy local execution and deployment to Google Cloud Run. Dockerfiles are provided for building container images for each service, facilitated by Google Cloud Build.

💡 Why it matters

The project demonstrates how distinct AI agents can collaborate in a specific domain (trading) using the A2A protocol. By separating trading logic from risk management into different agents that communicate securely and interoperably, the system showcases a modular approach to building multi-agent applications where each agent focuses on a specialized task.

#AIAgents #GoogleADK #A2AProtocol #TradingSimulation #FastAPI

Source: kweinmeister/agentic-trading

item.title: gym-pybullet-drones refactored for gymnasium and Betaflight SITL
item.description:
gym-pybullet-drones refactored for gymnasium and Betaflight SITL

A minimalist refactoring of the gym-pybullet-drones repository has been released to ensure compatibility with gymnasium, stable-baselines3 2.0, and betaflight SIM. The project, originally featured in GitHub’s Maintainer Spotlight 2026, now supports both single-agent and multi-agent tasks with updated system requirements.

🔍 Overview

  • Refactoring Goal: Minimalist update for compatibility with gymnasium, stable-baselines3 2.0, and betaflight SITL.
  • Version Control: The original IROS 2021 codebase is accessible via git checkout [paper|master].
  • Citation: Users are encouraged to cite the IROS 2021 paper and the original codebase.

🧩 How it works

  • Single-Agent Task: One drone hovers at z == 1.0.
  • Multi-Agent Task: Two drones hover at z == 1.2 and 0.7 respectively.
  • PettingZooWrapper: Exposes multi-drone aviary through PettingZoo’s Parallel API, assigning one agent per drone (drone_0, drone_1, …).
  • Observation and Reward: Each agent receives its own row of the aviary’s observation. The aviary’s team reward and episode flags are shared by all agents.
  • Centralized Critics: env.state() returns every drone’s kinematics for centralized critics.

⚙️ Key details

Requirement Details
Operating Systems Tested on Intel x64/Ubuntu 24.04 and Apple Silicon/macOS 26
Python & pybullet Requires Python 3.10+; pybullet has no pre-built wheel for versions beyond 3.10
Ubuntu Setup Install gcc to allow pip3 install to build pybullet
SITL Setup One-time setup requires building one SITL executable per drone from the repo’s top folder
Dependencies --num_drones must be less than or equal to the number passed to clone_bfs.sh; curl may be required via apt install

💡 Why it matters

The PettingZooWrapper makes the environment usable with Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL) libraries built on PettingZoo. The refactoring ensures the environment remains functional with modern reinforcement learning stacks like stable-baselines3 2.0 while supporting Betaflight SITL for drone simulation.

#gym-pybullet-drones #ReinforcementLearning #Multi-Agent #gymnasium #betaflight

Source: learnsyslab/gym-pybullet-drones

item.title: GRAIL Launches Digital Data Pipeline for Humanoid Robot Manipulation Training
item.description:
GRAIL Launches Digital Data Pipeline for Humanoid Robot Manipulation Training

🔍 Overview

GRAIL is a fully digital data-generation pipeline for humanoid loco-manipulation.

It composes 3D assets, simulator-ready scenes, robot-proportioned characters, and video foundation model priors to synthesize metric 4D human-object interaction (HOI) trajectories, then retargets them to a Unitree G1 and trains task-general policies for pick-up, whole-body manipulation, sitting, and terrain traversal.

🧩 How it works

The pipeline generates synthetic 4D human-object interaction trajectories using composed 3D assets and video foundation model priors, then retargets these to a Unitree G1 robot for policy training.

⚙️ Key details

  • Uses only GRAIL-generated data for training
  • Supports tasks: pick-up, whole-body manipulation, sitting, and terrain traversal
  • Policies transfer to real-world object pick-up and stair-climbing
  • Requires Linux GPU host with NVIDIA-enabled Docker
  • Examples include input videos in the GRAIL repository root
  • Two provider options: Kling (standard image) and MiniMax-H3 (nvgrail/grail:1.2.0-minimax-h3)
Component Description
3D Assets Composed with simulator-ready scenes
Video Priors Foundation model priors for interaction synthesis
Robot Unitree G1 for retargeting
Training Tasks Pick-up, whole-body manipulation, sitting, terrain traversal

🚀 Availability

  • Start in the GRAIL repository root on a Linux GPU host with NVIDIA-enabled Docker
  • Require Git LFS assets and reconstruction/retargeting submodules
  • Install guide available at docs/source/installation.md
  • First setup provisions workers in mounted checkout and cache
  • Robot stage needs SOMA Retargeter checkout, robot Python, and G1 assets
  • Retargeting setup documented at docs/source/installation.md#soma-retargeter-unitree-g1--dex3

💡 Why it matters

Using only GRAIL-generated data, the resulting egocentric visual policies transfer to real-world object pick-up and stair-climbing, demonstrating the pipeline’s effectiveness for real-world robot skill transfer.

#Robotics #Simulation #Humanoid #GRAIL #DataGeneration

Source: NVlabs/GRAIL

item.title: RealmForge: Open-Source Platform for Persistent Swarms of LLM Agents
item.description:
RealmForge: Open-Source Platform for Persistent Swarms of LLM Agents

RealmForge is an open‑source platform that orchestrates large swarms of LLM‑powered agents within a persistent, graph‑based world.

🔍 Overview

  • Open‑source platform for orchestrating vast swarms of LLM‑powered agents, each with unique identities, goals, and evolving relationships.
  • Operates within a Structured World Model that persists across sessions.
  • Moves beyond simple chat‑based interactions to emergent narratives, economies, and simulated societies.

🧩 Architecture

  • World Conductor service manages temporal flow, advancing the simulation in tick‑based cycles.
  • Chronicler module records all events into a searchable lore database.
  • Structured World Model (SWM) is a directed graph of entities (agents, locations, objects, concepts) with properties, inventory, and narrative history.
  • Relationship Graph decays over time if not reinforced, mimicking fading memory.
  • Narrative Market where agent desires act as bids for attention; the World Conductor selects the most pressing conflict or opportunity and creates a Plot Thread.
  • Environmental Events (e.g., storm, festival, dragon sighting) are generated based on internal clocks or random rolls.

⚙️ Agent Design

  • Each agent has a Persona Script (core traits, goals, knowledge cut‑off) and a State Vector (mood, health, inventory, relationships).
  • Agents possess a Perception Radius, limiting visibility and interaction to nearby entities in the graph, creating realistic information asymmetry.
  • Agents can delegate tasks to sub‑agents, enabling recursive complexity.
  • Language‑agnostic persona system; entities store language tags, allowing multilingual interaction through diplomat agents or translation artifacts.

📈 Persistence & Emergence

  • The world is a queryable knowledge graph, not a flat text string.
  • Time advances in discrete Epochs (configurable from seconds to months of in‑world time); agents act based on schedules, task durations, and information propagation.
  • The simulation tracks resource scarcity, faction reputation, and character development over simulated days or years.

📋 Core Components

Component Role
Structured World Model Directed graph storing entities, properties, inventory, and narrative history
World Conductor Advances simulation ticks, selects Plot Threads from Narrative Market
Chronicler Records all events into a searchable lore database
Relationship Graph Tracks relationships; decays over time without reinforcement
Narrative Market Hosts agent desires as bids for attention
Environmental Event Engine Generates storms, festivals, dragon sightings, etc.

#AI #OpenSource #AgentSimulation #KnowledgeGraph

Source: Abhinesh2004/mirage-cortex

item.title: Datawhale China Releases Alpha Version of Embodied AI Learning Platform with Online Simulation
item.description:
Datawhale China Releases Alpha Version of Embodied AI Learning Platform with Online Simulation

Datawhale China has launched an alpha internal test version of “Dive into Embodied AI” (具身智能), a comprehensive learning platform for embodied intelligent robot development. The platform covers the full “decision—control—perception” pipeline using reinforcement learning, world models, and VLA (Vision-Language-Action) methods across simulation environments, controllers, motion planning, and perception systems.

🔍 Overview

The platform is structured into four main sections:

  • Embodied Introduction (具身导论): Field overview with curated papers, datasets, open-source projects, and tools
  • Theoretical Foundation (理论基础): Core principles and concepts
  • Project Practice (项目实战): Hands-on projects organized by AMD Zone, Simulation Practice, and Real Machine Practice
  • Online Simulation (在线仿真): Interactive browser-based simulation environment

The release is labeled as an alpha internal test version, currently undergoing migration and restructuring with some chapters as placeholder pages. Users are encouraged to submit issues for feedback.

🧩 How it works

Online Simulation Features

The simulation environment (accessible at https://datawhalechina.github.io/dive-into-embodied-ai/simulation) provides:

  • Two modes: game-style free manipulation and policy demonstration
  • Pre-loaded policies:
    • Go2 and Pupper v3 PPO walking policies
    • Quaddle periodic gait comparison
    • MicroDuck head and full-body joint free manipulation (walking weights not yet available)
  • Controls: keyboard and on-screen directional buttons, pause, reset, slow simulation, camera follow
  • Go2 displays with simplified appearance using original collision model

Curriculum Structure

Embodied Introduction (7 chapters):

  1. What is Embodied AI — definition, perception-decision-action loop, body importance
  2. Development History — rule programming, model control, deep RL, and large model eras
  3. Robot Skills — tasks, grasping, manipulation, locomotion, navigation
  4. Embodied Carriers — humanoid, robotic arms, wheeled, quadruped, mobile manipulation, simulation bodies
  5. Core Challenges — data, sim-to-real, generalization, real-time, safety, evaluation
  6. Tech Stack — VLM, VLA, world models, manipulation, control, navigation modules
  7. Career Roles — brain algorithms, cerebellum algorithms, perception/navigation, engineering platforms, hardware

Project Practice Categories:

Category Projects
AMD Zone AUP Learning Cloud (Ryzen AI APU, ROCm, JupyterHub, Code Server); MicroDuck RL on AMD ROCm (R9700, ROCm MuJoCo Warp, dynamic contact regression, bipedal PPO); Pupper Quadruped on AMD (RL locomotion policies, VLA experiments)
Simulation Practice Build Quadruped from Scratch (MuJoCo, PD, kinematics, policy training, language control, perception); Petoi Quaddle Servo Walking (official URDF, alternating gait, contact verification, infinite checkerboard); MicroDuck RL (mjlab + MuJoCo Warp, GPU parallel PPO, bipedal gait); MuJoCo Arm with DDPG; ACT Bimanual Manipulation (ACT + ALOHA training, evaluation, reproduction)
Real Machine Practice LeRobot Chinese Course (Units 0-2: robot learning, datasets, toolchain, classic robotics); SO-101 + LeRobot Real Machine Tutorial (hardware connection, safety testing, action replay)

🚀 Availability

  • Platform language support: Chinese, English, Italian
  • Alpha version — active migration and restructuring in progress
  • Some chapters are placeholder pages
  • Model library integration planned (see simulation/README.md)
  • Tutorial and interactive pages include “Copy as Markdown” with Markdown preview dropdown

💡 Why it matters

This platform provides an end-to-end educational resource bridging theory and practice for embodied AI development, with particular emphasis on hardware-accessible projects (AMD ROCm support, real robot tutorials) and interactive browser-based simulation for immediate experimentation without local GPU setup.

#EmbodiedAI #Robotics #ReinforcementLearning #VLA #MuJoCo #Datawhale

Source: datawhalechina/dive-into-embodied-ai

item.title: Nebius Workbench Unifies Agent Control for Physical AI Workflows
item.description:
Nebius Workbench Unifies Agent Control for Physical AI Workflows

Nebius has established the Workbench endpoint as its agent control plane for Physical AI, providing a centralized infrastructure for managing robot policy training, simulation, and evaluation. This setup allows operators and coding agents to share authenticated connections for provisioning resources and executing complex AI workflows.

🧩 How it works

Workbench integrates a shared-access system where operators install the HTTPS service once, and users or coding agents connect using npa login with personal keys or Nebius human sign-in. The CLI and agents reuse this saved connection through a standardized API. For Kubernetes management, operators can utilize team namespaces and private SkyPilot contexts via the npa workbench namespace command.

⚙️ Key details

The agent control plane covers several core functions of the Physical AI stack:

  • Infrastructure setup and management
  • Simulation environments
  • Robot policy training
  • Synthetic data generation
  • Evaluation of model performance

Access to Workbench adds personal namespaces, GPU caps, and scoped storage. The architecture maps selected NVIDIA and open-ecosystem solutions to NPA’s public GHCR container catalog, specifically ghcr.io/nebius/nebius-physical-ai. Some images fetch models or vendor runtimes at execution time, with the packaging contract recording these boundaries.

Component Function
Workflow Engine Plans execution waves and submits them through SkyPilot
Token Factory Separate hosted inference API that supports direct calls without a cluster
Artifact Inspection Uses Rerun, Foxglove, media viewers, or reports to examine results
Simulation Environment Runs Unitree G1 policy rollouts in MJLab simulation

🚀 Availability

Developers can start with a shared-access quickstart for the Workbench endpoint. Coding agents such as Codex or Claude Code, when equipped with terminal access, use repository skills and npa to configure projects, provision GPU clusters and object storage, and run containerized tools. Operators managing Kubernetes directly can select namespaces and private SkyPilot contexts. Users remain in the loop for choices and human-bound approvals, such as accepting model terms.

#Nebius #PhysicalAI #Robotics #AIInfrastructure #CodingAgents

Source: nebius/nebius-physical-ai

item.title: Sovereign Core Unveils Open-Source AI-Driven Simulation Engine
item.description:
Sovereign Core Unveils Open-Source AI-Driven Simulation Engine

This week, Sovereign Core announced a new open‑source simulation platform that integrates a robust AI orchestration layer, a fault‑tolerant state grid, and a responsive command interface.

🔍 Overview

  • Provides a complete backend runtime, AI orchestration layer, and a responsive command interface for sovereign simulation environments.
  • Suitable for supply‑chain resilience, crisis response protocol testing, and synthetic training grounds for autonomous agents.
  • Delivers the structural integrity of a military‑grade simulation while remaining an open‑source framework.

🧩 How It Works

  • Fault‑tolerant grid distributes state, enabling operators to zoom from a macro‑level theater of operations down to individual asset behaviors without latency penalties.
  • Temporal event bus decouples simulation speed from rendering speed, allowing real‑time navigation of past, present, and speculative future states as layers.
  • The command interface is built on a reactive component architecture that consumes these layers without blocking input, ensuring fluid interaction even with tens of thousands of active entities.
  • A custom gleam‑engine propagates state updates in sub‑millisecond time across all connected clients.
  • A built‑in translation and localization pipeline supports English, Japanese, German, and Arabic, including a community‑driven framework for additional locales.
  • Natural‑language commands (voice or text) are parsed and executed in real time.
  • The UI adapts not only to screen size but also to operator role: logistics officers and tactical directors interact with different but synchronized control sets.

⚙️ Key Details

  • Cortical adapter treats the simulation as a sensorium for intelligent agents; the same APIs can be used by both human and AI operators.
  • The adapter allows pluggable backends—from lightweight heuristics to large language models running on private infrastructure.
  • An event‑sourced, lock‑free concurrency model underpins the simulation, making it a deterministic state machine that can be checkpointed, rewound, or forked.
  • Features speculative “what‑if” branches, scenario replay, and distributed computation across clusters.
  • The engine is written in a memory‑safe language with zero‑cost abstractions, enabling it to run on anything from a developer laptop to a dedicated server farm.
  • A built‑in health circuit monitors subsystems; upon failure (network partition, node crash, or data corruption), it automatically re‑routes and re‑establishes state, with structured, encrypted logs available for post‑mortem analysis.

🚀 Availability

  • The initial deployment package contains:
    • Core simulation runtime
    • Sample neural command agent
    • Bilingual (English / Japanese) interface template

💡 Why It Matters

  • The platform’s architecture allows for latency‑free, multi‑scale simulation, essential for realistic training and operational planning.
  • By integrating AI through a cortical adapter, future systems can expand to autonomous decision‑making within the same simulation environment.

#open-source #simulation #ai #distributed-systems #cognitive-computing

Source: endend2003-cmd/Tactical-Matrix-Console

item.title: Executing Isaac Sim Pick-and-Place Tasks Using SimReady Assets and Agent Controls
item.description:
Executing Isaac Sim Pick-and-Place Tasks Using SimReady Assets and Agent Controls

A walkthrough demonstrates a beverage can pick-and-place task in Isaac Sim using the UR17G arm, Robotiq 2F-140 gripper, and AI agent-generated controls. The workflow shows how to compose the scene, verify asset behaviors, and execute automated pick-and-place maneuvers.

🔍 Overview of SimReady Assets

For robotics workflows, a SimReady designation indicates an OpenUSD asset is prepared with properties needed for defined simulation use cases. Key aspects of the asset ecosystem include:

  • SimReady Foundation: Defines the required features an OpenUSD asset needs for a specific simulation use case.
  • SimReady Central: An open asset library hosted on Hugging Face that offers reusable robot and object assets along with authored simulation properties and profile-validation evidence.
  • Search Endpoints: Allows users to leverage the SimReady Central Space search service endpoint or USD Search endpoint to find OEM-curated content.

⚙️ Component Profiles and Settings

The pick-and-place example utilizes assets with validated simulation properties to establish a shared baseline for asset reuse:

Asset Profile Validated Properties Role in Simulation
UR17G Arm Robot-Body 4.0.0 Passing PhysX driven-joint checks (joint-drive settings) Executes arm movement and positioning
Robotiq 2F-140 Gripper Robot-Gripper 3.0.0 Passing PhysX driven-joint checks (joint-drive settings) Grasps and releases the beverage can
Beverage Can N/A Authored collisions and mass properties Rests on the work surface and serves as target object

🧩 Setup and Task Execution

The simulation workflow integrates scene assembly, system validation, and agent execution:

  • Asset Preparation: Download complete asset folders from SimReady Central (via direct download or Hugging Face CLI) so Isaac Sim can locate supporting files without missing-file errors.
  • Environment Launch: Start Isaac Sim version 6.2 from its installation directory with the remote Python server enabled (./isaac-sim.sh --enable isaacsim.code_editor.python_server).
  • Agent Configuration: Set up an agent configured with skills from the Agent Skills documentation. The model—such as GPT-6 Sol—executes Python against Isaac Sim to create and run the task code.
  • Scene & Task Definition: Assemble the work surface, arm-gripper assembly, and initial positions. Review joint limits, confirm the can rests on the surface without falling through, and configure controls to grasp, lift, move, and release the can.

#Robotics #IsaacSim #OpenUSD #SimReady #AIAgents

Source: Build a Robot Pick-and-Place Simulation with SimReady Assets

item.title: FoundationWorlds launches ToyBlocks simulation framework for robot learning
item.description:
FoundationWorlds launches ToyBlocks simulation framework for robot learning

Today a new framework called FoundationWorlds was introduced, pairing a controlled simulated world with tools for automatically generating tasks, training demonstrations, and metrics to measure a robot’s behavior over time.

🔍 Overview

  • The first FoundationWorld is ToyBlocks, an open simulation framework built around a robot arm and blocks on a tabletop.
  • ToyBlocks automatically generates demonstrations – recordings of a robot completing tasks in simulation – without requiring time‑consuming teleoperation.
  • It builds on earlier work in open robot learning, including MolmoAct 2, MolmoBot, and MolmoSpaces.

🧩 How it works

  • Skill generation uses reinforcement learning (RL) and motion planning in Isaac Lab, Nvidia’s open‑source framework for robot learning in simulation.
  • Policies learn non‑prehensile skills such as pushing a block across the table or flipping it onto another face without picking it up.
  • Skill generation can draw on privileged information (exact block position and orientation) that a real robot cannot sense, enabling automatic creation of skills that would otherwise need teleoperation.
  • A task‑and‑motion planner (TAMP) automatically selects and sequences skills to solve a task and plans the robot’s movements between them.
  • Each plan run in simulation produces a dataset of recorded demonstrations with labels describing the performed task or skill.
  • Data generation scales by running hundreds of plans in parallel on a single GPU, achieving up to 24 × real‑time performance.

⚙️ Key features

  • Designed around four requirements:
    1. Realistic physics and appearance
    2. Automatic generation of tasks and demonstrations at scale
    3. Challenges that combine reasoning with dexterity
    4. Broad coverage of the tasks possible within a domain
  • Blocks display pictures and letters, enabling searching, sorting, and arranging tasks.
  • A robot may need to turn a block to see a hidden face before deciding where it belongs.
  • Domain randomization varies block size, table height, and other physical properties from scene to scene to test generalization.
  • High‑level reasoning models decide what to do; low‑level action models control the robot’s movements.
  • Molmo 2 selects skills (e.g., rotation, flipping) via a pointing interface; ManiFlow executes the commanded skills on the simulated arm.
  • The controllable data generator lets users create training mixtures that emphasize particular skills or fill gaps in existing datasets.

💡 Why it matters

  • ToyBlocks gives researchers a way to study robotics questions in a deliberately constrained domain, providing realistic physics, automatic data generation, and a blend of reasoning and dexterity challenges.
  • By training models from raw sensor observations, the framework bridges the gap between simulation and real‑world perception problems.

#Robotics #Simulation #MachineLearning #AI

Source: ToyBlocks: A controlled world for robot learning and evaluation

item.title: NVIDIA Releases Four Open Cosmos 3‑Nano Checkpoints for Interactive World Simulation
item.description:
NVIDIA Releases Four Open Cosmos 3‑Nano Checkpoints for Interactive World Simulation

NVIDIA has added four open‑weight checkpoints to its Cosmos 3 model family, enabling interactive world simulation and multi‑sensor, multi‑view driving scene generation.

🔍 Overview

  • The new checkpoints are built on the Cosmos 3 Nano architecture and each contains 16 B trainable parameters.
  • All models are released under OpenMDW 1.1, which permits both commercial and non‑commercial use.
  • They target
    • offline synthetic driving data creation,
    • fast streaming simulation,
    • text‑guided visual rendering, and
    • bimanual robot interaction.

🧩 How it works

  • Cosmos3‑Nano‑Transfer‑Auto generates synchronized video from up to 11 camera views (including fisheyes) and joint RGB‑LiDAR data. It uses per‑camera World Scenario Map (WSM) controls for scene structure and traffic motion, while text prompts guide appearance.
  • Cosmos3‑Nano‑Sim‑Auto is a causally distilled streaming variant of Transfer‑Auto. It produces small chunks of synchronized camera video and LiDAR in a few denoising steps, leveraging generated history and updated driving controls for long, interactive rollouts. A simulation runtime and WSM renderer are required to update controls from driving inputs.
  • Cosmos3‑Nano‑Sim‑Transfer takes simulator controls and a text prompt to render photorealistic video observations. The physics and ground‑truth state remain with the simulator; the text prompt only influences appearance.
  • Cosmos3‑Nano‑Sim‑Bimanual predicts video based on robot or camera actions. It supports two‑arm simulation for YAM and AgiBot embodiments, controllable by a policy or human‑operated joysticks. Training used 59 control values padded to 64, with a schema that defines coordinate frames, rotations, gripper calibration, validity masks, and control domains.

⚙️ Key details

  • Open weight: All four checkpoints are open‑weight and can be post‑trained on user data to match specific camera layouts, LiDAR configurations, or environments.
  • Multi‑sensor sync: Camera and LiDAR streams are generated together, linking visual observations with 3‑D sensing.
  • Control flexibility: Scene and traffic‑signal controls let researchers vary road layouts and signal states, enabling study of driving‑policy responses.
  • Streaming interaction: Streaming generation ties video prediction to ongoing interaction, allowing exploration of how actions and observations unfold together.
  • Licensing: Released under OpenMDW 1.1, allowing commercial and non‑commercial use.

🚀 Availability

The four checkpoints—Cosmos3‑Nano‑Transfer‑Auto, Cosmos3‑Nano‑Sim‑Auto, Cosmos3‑Nano‑Sim‑Transfer, and Cosmos3‑Nano‑Sim‑Bimanual—are now available as open‑weight models in the Cosmos 3 family.

💡 Why it matters

  • Provides researchers with open tools for generating realistic driving data across many sensors and viewpoints.
  • Enables fast, interactive simulation of driving scenarios, supporting closed‑loop policy evaluation.
  • Extends simulation capabilities to robotic manipulation with bimanual actions, broadening the scope of world‑model research.
Model Primary capability
Cosmos3‑Nano‑Transfer‑Auto Offline multi‑view driving data generation with weather, lighting, text‑guided appearance, and joint RGB‑LiDAR sync
Cosmos3‑Nano‑Sim‑Auto Fast streaming of synchronized camera video and LiDAR for interactive driving rollouts
Cosmos3‑Nano‑Sim‑Transfer Convert simulator controls + text prompt into photorealistic video observations
Cosmos3‑Nano‑Sim‑Bimanual Predict video from bimanual robot actions; supports YAM and AgiBot two‑arm embodiments

#NVIDIA #WorldSimulation #OpenModels #AI #LiDAR

Source: New NVIDIA Cosmos 3 Open Models for Interactive World Simulation

item.title: NVIDIA RTX Spark and Isaac Lab Enable Simulated Navigation Training for Microduck Robot
item.description:
NVIDIA RTX Spark and Isaac Lab Enable Simulated Navigation Training for Microduck Robot

NVIDIA demonstrated an end‑to‑end workflow that uses RTX Spark, Isaac Lab, and Omniverse tools to create a simulated obstacle course, train a navigation policy for the Microduck robot, and evaluate the policy in Isaac Sim.

🔍 Overview

  • Teaching a robot to navigate an obstacle course requires perception, balance, and the ability to adjust actions when obstacles block the path ahead, not just a walking policy.
  • The development process links three stages: creating assets and an environment, using physics simulation to model robot‑environment interaction, and training + evaluating policies in simulation.

🛠️ Tools and Roles

Component Role
RTX Spark Local development hub; supports AI‑assisted planning, policy validation, and receives trained policies for local evaluation in Isaac Sim.
Isaac Lab Cloud‑based robot‑learning framework for reinforcement learning.
Newton Models physical behavior for simulation.
Omniverse libraries Generate simulated visual observations via RTX rendering.
Isaac Sim Runs local evaluation of trained policies returned from RTX Spark.
Hermes Translates prompts into step‑by‑step project plans and creates asset inventories from images.
NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Bolt Works with Hermes to generate project plans and analyze images for reusable assets.
Astra Builds and tests assets; directs FreeCAD geometry creation and Blender material application.
SimReady Central Library Free, ungated library of >2,000 simulation‑ready OpenUSD assets.
Microduck Reference quadruped robot used for navigation training.

📐 Workflow Steps

  1. Write a natural‑language prompt that describes the obstacle course and what Microduck must learn.
  2. On RTX Spark, Hermes and NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Bolt translate the prompt into a detailed project plan (task, resources, outputs, stages).
  3. Review official Microduck documentation and summarize its capabilities, constraints, and unknowns.
  4. Define the course layout, obstacle dimensions, clearances, and intended route.
  5. Generate a photorealistic concept image using a verified Microduck reference image.
  6. Hermes and Nemotron analyze the concept image, extract unique reusable assets, assign identifiers, and create cropped reference images.
  7. Astra enhances the references, models geometry in FreeCAD, and adds fine details and materials in Blender.
  8. Assemble the assets into a simulated environment; Newton provides physics, Omniverse renders visuals.
  9. Train a navigation policy with Isaac Lab in the cloud using the simulated environment.
  10. Return the trained policy to RTX Spark and evaluate it locally in Isaac Sim.
  11. Verify robot capabilities, test navigation, obstacle handling, and reset logic—all in simulation (no physical hardware).
  12. Package the plan, robot brief, concept, asset inventory, crops, and execution instructions for reproducibility.

📊 What You’ll Learn

  • How to create a simulated obstacle course for a quadruped robot.
  • How AI agents (Hermes, Nemotron, Astra) automate planning, asset extraction, and 3D modeling.
  • How to train a navigation policy with Isaac Lab and validate it with RTX Spark and Isaac Sim.
  • How to leverage the SimReady Central Library for reusable simulation assets.

#NVIDIA #Robotics #Simulation #ReinforcementLearning #AIAgents

item.title: Skild AI launches S1, a video‑to‑robot foundation model for manipulation
item.description:
Skild AI launches S1, a video‑to‑robot foundation model for manipulation

🔍 Overview

Skild AI unveiled S1 in August 2026 as its flagship foundation model for robotic manipulation. The system can learn a new task from a single video demonstration without any additional task‑specific training or weight adjustments.

🧩 How S1 Works

  • The model receives a video showing a task and then attempts to replicate the observed task using a robot, without modifying its weights or requiring a specific post‑training phase.
  • S1 is trained using episodes in which a visual demonstration describes the task to be performed.
  • It learns to relate what it observes in the video to the current scene and the available motor controls, reconstructing an action policy that achieves the same goal with its own robotic body.
  • Pre‑training combines several data types: teleoperation, first‑person human videos, simulation, and experiments conducted on robots.
  • Several scenarios did not appear in the pre‑training data; basic gestures are combined into novel sequences.

📊 Performance Metrics

  • On unseen tasks lasting four to eight minutes, trained on a reported 100,000 hours of data, S1 achieved an average cumulative success rate per step of 66 %, compared with 9 % for a linguistic baseline.
  • The metric aggregates the success rates of the various stages; it does not represent a 66 % success rate for each mission.
  • Human intervention was used to reset the system after a failure so that all stages could be evaluated.
  • A real‑world demonstration is estimated to be equivalent to approximately 380 post‑training sessions on the tasks studied.

🛠️ Supporting Infrastructure

Component Role
Cosmos Organizes and enriches video data
Omniverse Provides virtual environments
Isaac Sim Provides virtual environments
Isaac Lab Used for reinforcement learning
TensorRT Optimizes inference

On September 10 2026 NVIDIA detailed this infrastructure, highlighting how Cosmos, Omniverse, Isaac Sim, Isaac Lab, and TensorRT work together to train, simulate, and deploy S1.

🚀 Availability

  • S1 is available through select deployments and partnerships, not as a freely downloadable model.

💡 Why It Matters

  • Enables robots to acquire new manipulation skills from a single video, dramatically reducing the data collection and training time required for each new task.
  • Demonstrated capabilities include repotting a plant, making filter coffee, making pancakes, and assembling a kit, with sequences lasting up to ten minutes and involving several successive gestures.
  • For the repotting task, the company reports that it went from recording the demonstration to beginning autonomous execution in eleven minutes.
  • The same set of weights generates all the examples shown, confirming the model’s ability to generalize across diverse tasks.

#SkildAI #Robotics #FoundationModel #Simulation

Source: 5 Steps to Create SimReady Assets for Robotics with Frontier AI Models | NVIDIA Technical Blog Source: Skild AI’s S1: Learning a Robotic Task from a Video

item.title: Introduction of SimLife Platform and SimLife-BP Behavioral Pattern Benchmark
item.description:
Introduction of SimLife Platform and SimLife-BP Behavioral Pattern Benchmark

Researchers have introduced SimLife, a scalable platform designed to simulate long-term household life, alongside a corresponding benchmark called SimLife-BP to evaluate long-context pattern understanding.

🔍 Overview

SimLife is a simulation platform that provides:

  • Rich visual observations
  • Ground-truth action logs
  • Synthetic dialogues with audio

⚙️ Key details

SimLife-BP is used to evaluate the ability to infer latent behavioral rules from observations spanning weeks or months. The benchmark consists of:

  • 106 episodes
  • 1,439 question-answer pairs
  • Average episode length of 15.49 hours and 38.57 in-game days

🧩 How it works

Tasks within the benchmark probe the following types of reasoning under various levels of rule hints:

  • Direct reasoning
  • Counterfactual reasoning
  • Noisy reasoning
  • Inverse reasoning

💡 Why it matters

Evaluations of frontier models and architectures revealed several limitations in current AI capabilities:

  • Models often achieve surface-level prediction instead of comprehensive rule understanding.
  • Models rely on frequency-based heuristics rather than if-then reasoning based on evidence.
  • Models struggle to adapt when behavioral patterns change.

#SimLife #AIbenchmarks #LongContext #BehavioralModeling

Source: SIMLIFE: Pattern Understanding for Long-Horizon Human-Agent Partnership
